keyVerseText: And it came to pass, when Rehoboam had established the kingdom, and had strengthened himself, he forsook the law of the LORD, and all Israel with him.
rootMeaning: The root of חֶזְקָה (chezqâh) is חֵזֶק (chêzeq), which fundamentally denotes strength or help. As the feminine form, חֶזְקָה carries the sense of strength or force, emphasizing a prevailing power or the act of strengthening oneself. This root sense highlights not just physical power but also the capacity to uphold, sustain, or exert influence, which goes beyond the common English gloss of 'strength' by implying an active, prevailing force or urgency.
usageInScripture: The word חֶזְקָה appears four times in Scripture, consistently conveying the idea of strength or being strong, whether in a personal, prophetic, or royal context. Its translations range from 'and had strengthened' to 'by his strength,' revealing a consistent theme of empowerment or prevailing force. This range shows that חֶזְקָה is used both to describe internal strength, such as self-strengthening, and external manifestations of power, such as royal authority or prophetic inspiration.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding חֶזְקָה enriches our grasp of biblical strength as more than mere physical might; it involves spiritual empowerment and divine enablement. The word's use in prophetic and royal contexts underscores that true strength is ultimately derived from God’s hand and authority. For the Christian faith, this reminds believers that genuine strength comes from reliance on God, who empowers His people to stand firm and fulfill His purposes. It also warns against self-reliance that leads away from obedience to the Lord, highlighting the necessity of humility and dependence on divine strength.
keyVerseReflection: In 2 Chronicles 12:1, the phrase 'and had strengthened himself' uses חֶזְקָה to describe Rehoboam's act of establishing his kingdom through his own strength. This word underscores the human effort and prevailing power he exerted. However, the verse also reveals the consequence of this self-strengthening—forsaking the law of the LORD—teaching that reliance on one’s own strength apart from God leads to spiritual failure and communal downfall.
